problems.title: Fewer, fatter loads
problems.statement: 256 threads load a 128 × 8 float tile (1,024 floats).
problems.solution: 4 versus 1. Same bytes, same sectors, a quarter of the instructions.

problems.title: Alignment
problems.statement: A row-major float matrix with K columns, loaded with float4s along rows from a 16-byte-aligned base.

parts.prompt: For which K is every float4 aligned?

hints: Row starts must be multiples of 16 bytes: K a multiple of 4.
problems.solution: 1000 and 1024 are multiples of 4. For other sizes, libraries pad, or take a scalar path for the misaligned edges.

problems.title: What double buffering saves
problems.statement: Per K-step: loading the next tiles takes 400 cycles of latency; computing on the current tiles takes 300 cycles.
hints: Overlapped: the longer of the two.
problems.solution: (a) 700. (b) max(400, 300) = 400: now load-bound. (c) 1.75×. If compute were longer than the load, double buffering would hide the load completely.

problems.title: How many stages?
problems.statement: With s stages, loads are issued s − 1 steps ahead. Load latency 600 cycles, compute per step 200 cycles.

parts.prompt: Minimum stages to hide the latency?
If compute per step doubles to 400?

problems.solution: (a) $s - 1 \ge 3$: 4 stages. (b) $s - 1 \ge 1.5$: 3. Faster math (tensor cores) needs deeper pipelines, which is why Hopper kernels run 4–7 stages.

problems.title: The shared-memory bill
problems.solution: 32 KB, 16 KB, and 64 KB for 4 stages: the whole of a GW-1 SM's shared memory. Stages compete with tile size and residency for the same storage.

problems.title: Registers for register-staged prefetch
problems.statement: Without cp.async, double buffering goes global → registers → shared. A 256-thread block prefetches 128 × 8 A values and 8 × 128 B values per step.

parts.prompt: Extra registers per thread to hold the prefetched values?

problems.solution: 8 floats per thread (two float4s). On a kernel already near 128 registers, that can cost occupancy or cause spills, which is part of why cp.async (straight to shared memory) matters.

problems.title: Barriers per step
hints: With two stages, one barrier separates writing the next stage from reading it.
problems.solution: 2 and 1. Writes to the next stage can't conflict with reads of the current one, so one of the two barriers disappears.

problems.title: Bytes in flight per SM
problems.statement: The GW-1's 512 GB/s shared evenly by 16 SMs at 1.5 GHz, 400-cycle latency.

parts.prompt: Bytes each SM must keep in flight?
Does one 8 KB stage in flight for each of 2 resident blocks suffice? (1 = yes, 0 = no)

problems.solution: (a) 8,533 bytes. (b) 16 KB in flight > 8.5 KB: yes. A double-buffered GEMM with a couple of blocks per SM keeps memory busy.

problems.title: Copying a tile: threads versus TMA
problems.statement: A 128 × 32 FP16 tile (8 KB), copied global → shared by 128 threads with 16-byte loads and stores.
problems.solution: 1,024 instructions versus one TMA instruction from one thread (plus a barrier wait). Freeing the threads from copying is what lets Hopper kernels specialise warps into producers and consumers.

problems.title: Declaring overlap
problems.statement: The simulator can't detect overlap, so you declare ilp.

options: Whenever the kernel uses shared memory
When the loop issues the next stage's loads before the current stage's math
When the kernel has two loops

hints: The loads must actually be in flight during the math.
problems.solution: Only when the code really has two independent requests outstanding. A declared overlap the code doesn't have gives you a number the hardware won't reproduce.
